asRun.standInNote: The runnable adapter fits two real Tweedie regressions with a logarithm link at the chosen variance power, one on the up part of the scaled move and one on the down part, each zero whenever the move went the other way, and reads the probability of up as the chance that the up part is not zero divided by the sum of that chance for both parts. The family and the fit match the specification, but the zero here marks the sign of the move rather than the absence of an event, and the as-run numbers measure that share of two zero masses, which is expected to stay close to one half.
asRun.probabilityNote: Each side's fitted mean, variance power and Pearson dispersion give the compound Poisson-Gamma probability that the side is exactly zero, and the probability of up is one minus the up side's zero mass divided by the sum of one minus each side's zero mass, with no curve fitted afterwards.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per bar, one value for the single fit

meaningful.why: The probability is read straight from the two fitted Tweedie zero masses with nothing tuned on validation bars, so this number on unseen bars is the direct test of whether the share of those two masses is an honest statement of the odds of a higher close.

Even when the share of zero masses hugs one half its ordering can carry information, and this number tests whether bars where the up part is more likely to be non-zero than the down part are more often followed by a higher close.

The engine goes long when the up part is at least as likely to be non-zero as the down part and short otherwise, and this is what that rule earned after costs beyond holding the same contract through the same folds.

It is the money made by trading the side whose Tweedie model gives the smaller zero mass, under the engine's fill and exit rule with costs charged, read beside the predicted up share and the trade count.
It relates the per-bar profit of following the smaller of the two zero masses to its bumpiness; zero is only an arithmetic marker because a coin-flip trader still pays costs.
Because the two zero masses sit close together, a small drift in one fitted dispersion can hold the call on one side for a long stretch, and this shows the deepest loss such a stretch produced.
It compares winning with losing trades opened when the share of the two zero masses crossed one half, after costs; one is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill level.
It counts the share of trades begun at a flip between the up part and the down part that closed with a profit, and must be read with average win and loss because exits follow the engine's rule.

It is the hit rate of calling up when the up part's chance of being non-zero is at least the down part's; the fit is unweighted, so the cut follows the training mix of up and down moves and the reference is the majority-class accuracy.

With probabilities close to one half a small tilt in the two intercepts sends nearly every bar to one side, and averaging the hit rate over up bars and down bars shows whether the features move the call at all.
It condenses the four counts of called against actual direction into one symmetric number that stays near zero when the contest between the two zero masses is decided by their intercepts alone.

It grades the share of the two zero masses on a bounded squared scale; because that share rarely leaves the neighbourhood of one half, the reading sits near that of quoting one half and the gap to it is the information.

Nothing is fitted on validation bars and no class weights are used, so the binned gap between the share of zero masses and the observed up share is a fair check of the bridge's own odds, read with the count of occupied bins because the probabilities cluster.
The share of two zero masses is not a likelihood of the up label, so nothing forces its scale to be right; this slope shows whether the odds it states are too timid or too bold on unseen bars.
The registry note expects probabilities close to one half, and the spread of the probability shows how far the fitted means and dispersions ever move the share away from it.

The forecast is the fitted mean of the up part minus the fitted mean of the down part from the same pair of Tweedie fits run a second time for the price role, which is the model's expected move, so skill against the no-change forecast tests the size models directly.
The difference of the two fitted means targets the average move and not the middle one, and squared-error skill against the no-change forecast is the consistent score for an average.
It is the average miss in points of the up mean minus the down mean, read against the no-change error on the same bars because both parts are capped at a high training percentile before fitting.

The forecast's sign says which part has the larger expected size while the traded call says which part is more likely to be non-zero, so this hit rate tests the size contest separately from the zero-mass contest, shown with its denominator.
A side can have the larger expected size and still the larger zero mass when its dispersion is higher, and this share shows how often the forecast line and the traded call point the same way.

It is the score on inner blocks of the training span that chose the variance power and the penalty strength; it is a selection score, optimistic by construction, and not the held-out deviance the specification profiles the power on.

The single fit is reported as one step and carries only a validation value, the logarithmic loss of the share of the two Tweedie zero masses on the validation bars; nothing is fitted on those bars, so the value is fully out of sample for the fit, and no training value is reported beside it.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The adapter reports no training loss for the single fit, because the two Tweedie fits are not scored on the training rows, so there is no training value to subtract from the validation value.
With long-only off and no stop or target the engine is always in a position once it has traded, so the share of bars held describes the engine's rule and not the Tweedie fits.

caveats: The up part and the down part of one move are never both non-zero, yet the probability of up combines two separately fitted zero masses as if they were unrelated, so the share is a model-implied number and not a fitted likelihood of the up label.

The zero in each fitted target marks a move that went the other way, not the absence of an event as in the specification, so the fitted zero mass is close to the share of opposite-sign moves and the probabilities stay near one half.
The variance power is chosen by the engine's shared search on a trading score over inner training blocks, not by held-out Tweedie deviance as the specification describes.
Consecutive bars share most of the bars inside their label horizon, so any interval on these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance, never a binomial interval.

The trading numbers depend on the run's long-only switch, holding bars, stop, target and contract count, which are recorded with each run; costs for roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract reuse that contract's account figures as a stated assumption, and the last bar of a fold exits at its close.

zero_inflated_poisson.summary: Counts the large up bars and the large down bars expected in the next h bars, allowing extra 'quiet market' zeros; the side expected to have more sets the direction.
zero_inflated_poisson.implementationNote: Bridge: fitted twice (up and down impulse counts); direction is the contest of the two expected counts, calibrated on validation. Differs from the spec: a failed zero-inflated fit falls back to Poisson, logged. Expect: it predicts which side has more large bars, not the sign of the h-bar move.

impulse_multiple.label: Impulse size (x bar scale)
impulse_multiple.description: A bar counts as an impulse when its move is beyond this multiple of the trailing one-bar scale.

max_iterations.label: Maximum iterations
max_iterations.description: The most steps the solver takes to find the weights.

native.produces: For every bar a probability that the count is a structural zero, a Poisson rate for the bars where activity can happen, and the combined expected count, which is the rate times the chance that the bar is not a structural zero.
native.targetVariable: A whole-number count of events per bar or session with more exact zeros than one Poisson rate can produce, such as block trades or stop-run events
native.objectiveNote: The likelihood here is a two-part blend, a point mass at zero chosen through a logistic link and a Poisson count through a logarithm link, so it is not a single exponential family and is fitted by expectation-maximisation or by direct maximisation of the blended likelihood.

metrics.why: Both sets of weights, the ones for the structural-zero switch and the ones for the Poisson rate, are fitted to maximise one blended likelihood, so the deviance under that zero-inflated distribution on later bars is the fitted quantity measured out of sample.
metrics.baseline: The same deviance for the zero-inflated fit with intercepts only on the same training rows

metrics.why: The whole reason for the model is the extra zero switch, and the specification requires a test against the plain Poisson fit first; the held-out deviance of this model minus that of the same rate model with the switch removed says whether the second set of weights corrected a bias or only added variance.
metrics.baseline: The plain Poisson regression on the same features and the same bars

metrics.why: The blended likelihood can match the average count while splitting it wrongly between the structural-zero switch and the rate, and placing each realised count inside its predicted distribution shows whether the predicted share of zeros matches the observed one.
metrics.baseline: The flat histogram a correctly specified count distribution gives

metrics.why: On bars the switch marks as active the model promises Poisson-sized scatter around the rate, so a band from the full zero-inflated distribution should hold the realised count as often as its level says.
metrics.baseline: The nominal level of each plotted band

metrics.why: Once the excess zeros are absorbed by the switch, the remaining counts are still assumed to have variance equal to their rate; a ratio above one on the active bars points to the zero-inflated negative binomial variant.
metrics.baseline: One, the value when the active-bar counts spread as a Poisson rate says

metrics.why: Quiet stretches and active stretches come in runs, so residuals of the combined expected count that stay correlated across bars mean the switch is missing a persistence that a trailing rolling mean count already carries.

notApplicable.name: Directional Edge
notApplicable.why: A hit rate on the sign of a forward return never applied to a model that predicts how many events occur and whether any can occur.

notApplicable.name: Confidence Edge
notApplicable.why: Ranking up bars above down bars is not what a structural-zero probability or a Poisson rate does, so the metric never applied.

notApplicable.name: Gaussian NLL Loss
notApplicable.why: The stamped Gaussian objective is not this model's objective; it maximises the blended zero-and-Poisson likelihood, which the native record grades with the deviance of that distribution.

notApplicable.name: Volatility-Adjusted RMSE
notApplicable.why: It grades a return forecast scaled by volatility, while the native output is an expected count scored on the count scale.

notApplicable.name: Top-Decile Directional Edge
notApplicable.why: No registry metric scores only the most confident tenth of direction calls, and a count model makes no direction call to restrict.

notApplicable.name: Brier Score
notApplicable.why: The registry's Brier score is against the up or down outcome, and this model states no probability of up; its structural-zero probability is checked against the observed zero share instead.

notApplicable.name: Directional accuracy
notApplicable.why: A count of block trades or stop runs has no up or down side, so there is no direction call until a bridge sets an up-side count model against a down-side one.

notApplicable.name: Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve
notApplicable.why: The outputs order bars by expected activity and by the chance of no activity, not by direction, so there are no up and down classes to rank.

notApplicable.name: Gaussian negative log-likelihood
notApplicable.why: A Gaussian density cannot hold a lump of probability at exactly zero or whole-number outcomes, which are the two features this model is built around.

notApplicable.name: Volatility-adjusted root mean square error
notApplicable.why: Natively the forecast is a count and not a price move, so an error in points of a return forecast has nothing to measure.

notApplicable.name: Brier score
notApplicable.why: The only probability the model states is that of a structural zero, not of an up bar, so the engine's squared error against the direction outcome does not grade it.

notApplicable.name: Sharpe ratio
notApplicable.why: A count forecast takes no position; the ratio appears only after the bridge compares two expected counts and the engine trades the result with costs.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable adapter fits two real zero-inflated Poisson models, one on the count of large up bars and one on the count of large down bars inside the label horizon, where large means a one-bar move beyond the impulse multiple times the trailing bar scale, then takes the logarithm of the ratio of the two expected counts as a score and maps it to a probability with a logistic curve fitted on validation bars; a side whose zero-inflated fit fails falls back to a plain Poisson fit and logs a warning. The specification forecasts event counts and has no direction, so every as-run number measures two count models plus that readout, and it predicts which side has more large bars, not the sign of the move over the horizon.
asRun.probabilityNote: Each side's expected count is its Poisson rate times one minus its structural-zero probability, the score is the logarithm of the up expected count minus the logarithm of the down expected count, and a two-parameter logistic curve fitted on the fold's validation labels maps that score to the probability of up.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per bar, one value for the single fit

meaningful.why: It grades the odds that come out of the expected-count ratio after the validation-fitted logistic curve, so it tests the two zero-inflated models and the curve together; the curve's slope and intercept saw validation bars, and only the test walk is fully out of sample.

The logistic curve only stretches or flips the score, so this number tests the impulse contest itself: whether bars where large up bars are expected to outnumber large down bars by more are more often followed by a higher close at the label horizon.

The engine goes long when the curved expected-count ratio is at least one half and short otherwise, and this is what that rule earned after costs beyond holding the same contract through the same folds.
It is the money made by trading the side expected to have more impulse bars, under the engine's fill and exit rule with costs charged, read beside the predicted up share and the trade count.

It relates the per-bar profit of following the contest between expected up impulses and expected down impulses to its bumpiness; zero is only an arithmetic marker because a coin-flip trader still pays costs.
It shows the deepest loss run while the contest of expected large-bar counts, which combines the structural-zero switch and the Poisson rate on each side, pointed the wrong way.
It compares winning with losing trades opened when the curved expected-count ratio crossed one half, after costs; one is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill level.
It counts the share of trades begun at a flip of the impulse contest that closed with a profit, and must be read with average win and loss because exits follow the engine's rule.

It is the hit rate of calling up when the curved expected-count ratio is at least one half; the cut reflects the intercept the curve learned on validation bars, and the reference is the majority-class accuracy.

When impulses are rare on both sides the ratio of expected counts barely moves and the curve's intercept decides the call, and averaging the hit rate over up bars and down bars shows whether anything but that intercept is at work.
It condenses the four counts of called against actual direction into one symmetric number that stays near zero when the expected up and down impulse counts rarely differ enough to move the call.

The logarithm of a ratio of two small expected counts can swing widely, and a bounded squared score keeps the reading from hinging on the few bars where the curve turned such a swing into near-certain odds.

The logistic curve was fitted without class weights on validation outcomes, so the binned gap between stated and observed up share checks whether a mapping learned on the validation span still holds on the test span, read with the count of occupied bins.

The forecast is the expected up impulse count minus the expected down impulse count times one scale factor fitted through the origin on training rows, so skill against the no-change forecast tests whether an imbalance of large bars carries over to the size of the move.
It is the average miss in points of the scaled difference of expected impulse counts, read against the no-change error on the same bars because bars below the impulse size are ignored by the counts.

The forecast's sign is the sign of the expected-count difference times the fitted scale factor, so this is the hit rate of the raw impulse contest before the validation curve shifts it, shown with its denominator.

The traded call is the curved logarithm of the expected-count ratio while the forecast line is the scaled difference, so a share below one shows how often the curve's intercept or a negative slope overruled the side the two expected counts favoured.

If the structural-zero switches on both sides react to the same quiet-market features, the ratio of expected counts cancels and the spread of the probability shows that the output never leaves the neighbourhood of one half.
It is the score on inner blocks of the training span that chose the impulse multiple, which decides what counts as a large bar; it is a selection score, optimistic by construction, and not a result.

The single fit is reported as one step and carries only a validation value, the logarithmic loss of the curved expected-count probability of up on the validation bars; the logistic curve was fitted on those same bars, so the value is partly in-sample and no training value is reported beside it.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: The adapter reports no training loss for the single fit, because the two zero-inflated fits are not scored on the training rows, so there is no training value to subtract from the validation value.
With long-only off and no stop or target the engine is always in a position once it has traded, so the share of bars held describes the engine's rule and not the count models.

caveats: The fitted target is the count of bars whose one-bar move exceeds the impulse multiple times the trailing bar scale, so the model learns which side has more large bars and not whether the close at the label horizon is higher.

A side whose zero-inflated fit raises an error, fails to converge or gives non-finite weights is replaced by a plain Poisson fit with no structural-zero switch; the run log and the fit summary say which side fell back, and the numbers of such a fold describe a mixed pair of models.
The impulse multiple that defines the counted event is chosen by the engine's shared search on a trading score, so the target itself changes from fold to fold.

The logistic curve's slope and intercept are fitted on the fold's validation rows, so validation loss is partly in-sample for those two numbers and a negative fitted slope inverts the impulse contest.
Consecutive bars share most of the bars inside their label horizon, so any interval on these numbers needs a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance, never a binomial interval.

The trading numbers depend on the run's long-only switch, holding bars, stop, target and contract count, which are recorded with each run; costs for roots other than the Micro Nasdaq contract reuse that contract's account figures as a stated assumption, and the last bar of a fold exits at its close.

multivariate_regression.summary: Forecasts the move at several horizons at once from the same features, sharing their errors; P(up) is the chance the h-bar forecast lands above zero.
multivariate_regression.implementationNote: Bridge: ridge on J horizons h/J..h with the residual covariance; P(up) = Phi(y_h / sd_h). Differs from the spec: only the h-bar column is scored; the others act through the shared covariance and the optional reduced rank. Expect: close to ridge regression with a probability of its own.

horizon_count.label: Horizons
horizon_count.description: How many horizons up to h are forecast together.

reduced_rank.label: Reduced rank
reduced_rank.description: Rank of the coefficient matrix; 0 keeps the full rank.

penalty_strength.label: Penalty strength
penalty_strength.description: Ridge penalty added to X'X; larger is simpler.

native.produces: For every bar it outputs a forecast for each of several linked targets at once from one shared set of features, together with a covariance matrix that says how the forecast errors of those targets move together.
native.targetVariable: The expected values of several correlated continuous outcomes for the same bar, such as the price moves over several forward horizons, and the joint spread of their forecast errors
native.objectiveNote: Under Gaussian errors the joint likelihood is maximised by the same least squares coefficients each target would get alone, so what this model's version adds is the residual covariance across targets estimated afterwards from the fitted misses, and an optional low-rank constraint that makes the targets share a few feature combinations.

metrics.why: The model's claim is a joint Gaussian with a fitted mean per target and a residual covariance across targets, so the log of that density at the moves which really happened is the one score that grades the coefficient matrix and the covariance together.
metrics.baseline: The same density score from the training rows' average move and their raw covariance with no features.

metrics.why: Read one target at a time, each forecast is a bell curve centred on the fitted line with the residual spread of that target, and this score charges for both a misplaced centre and a spread that is too wide or too narrow.
metrics.baseline: The same score for a bell curve centred on no move with the training rows' spread of that target.

metrics.why: Each column of the coefficient matrix is a least squares line for one target, so its squared miss on unseen bars beside the miss of forecasting no move shows whether the centre of the bell curve carries anything before the covariance is considered.
metrics.baseline: The no-change forecast on the same resolved bars.

metrics.why: The specification asks for a per-target miss beside the joint one, and this is that miss for one target in chart units, which on its own says nothing about the covariance the model was built to add.
metrics.baseline: The root mean square size of the actual move on the same bars.

metrics.why: The residual covariance turns each forecast into an ellipsoid across targets and a band for each one, and counting how often realised moves land inside those bands at each plotted level tests the covariance directly.
metrics.baseline: The nominal level of each plotted band.

metrics.why: Feeding each realised move through its own forecast bell curve should give evenly spread values, and a pile-up at the two ends would show that the fat tails of futures moves break the Gaussian error assumption behind the covariance.

Position sizing leans on the fitted residual covariance, so the share of refits in which each cross-target correlation keeps its sign shows whether that covariance is a property of the market or of one training span.

notApplicable.name: Directional Edge
notApplicable.why: The joint fit forecasts the size of several targets and never an up or down class, so a direction hit rate was never a native score of it.

notApplicable.name: Confidence Edge
notApplicable.why: No class probability exists natively, so conviction deciles had nothing to be formed from.

notApplicable.name: Top-Decile Directional Edge
notApplicable.why: No registry metric restricts scoring to the most confident tenth of bars, and the joint fit carries no direction natively.

notApplicable.name: Brier Score
notApplicable.why: The model outputs sizes and an error covariance and no probability of an event, so a squared probability error had nothing to be computed on natively.

asRun.standInNote: The runnable adapter fits a closed-form ridge regression of the volatility-scaled moves at several horizons up to the label horizon on the same standardised features and estimates their residual covariance, which is the ridge multi-horizon case the specification describes, but only the label-horizon column is forecast and scored and the probability of up is the area above zero of that column's own Gaussian forecast, so the as-run numbers measure one column of the joint model and never the joint forecast across targets.
asRun.probabilityNote: The probability of up is the standard normal area above zero of the label-horizon forecast divided by its predictive standard deviation, which is the training residual standard deviation of that horizon widened by the bar's leverage under the ridge-penalised feature matrix; no curve is fitted and no class weights are used.

stepQuantity.unit: nats per bar, one value for the single fit, on the validation rows only, because the closed-form fit returns no training loss; it is the plain logarithmic loss of the model's own Gaussian tail-area probability of up, with no curve and no class weights

meaningful.why: The probability of up is read straight off the model's own Gaussian forecast for the label horizon with no curve in between, so this score tests the fitted centre and the residual spread together, with the fold's training up share quoted on every bar as the reference.

The label-horizon column of the ridge coefficient matrix minimises penalised squared misses, so its squared miss against forecasting no move on resolved bars is the matching test of the centre of the forecast; it is derived from the recorded forecasts and not printed by the engine.

The engine goes long whenever the label-horizon forecast is above zero, because that is when the Gaussian area above zero reaches one half, and this is what those calls earned after costs beyond holding the same contract through the same folds.

The odds come from dividing the forecast by its own predictive standard deviation, so a slope below one says that deviation is too small for the true uncertainty of the move and a slope above one says it is too wide.
It grades the same Gaussian tail area on a bounded squared scale, and because the fit is unweighted and uses no curve the value can be read against always quoting the fold's training up share.

No class weights and no validation curve touch the tail area, so a gap between stated and observed up share is the model's own; it is read with the occupied-bin count because a small forecast beside a large residual spread keeps most bars near one half.
Dividing by the predictive standard deviation reorders bars only through their leverage, so this number mostly tests whether a larger label-horizon ridge forecast goes with bars that went up.
The ridge forecast is small beside the residual spread of the move, so the Gaussian tail area rarely strays far from one half, and this spread shows how much the model ever commits.

It compares the absolute miss of the label-horizon ridge forecast, after tick rounding, with forecasting no move, and is read beside the squared version because the line itself targets the average move.
It gives the typical miss of the label-horizon forecast in points after the scaled output is multiplied back by the trailing move scale, read beside the no-change forecast's miss on the same bars.

With no curve between forecast and call, the sign of the price forecast and the traded side come from the same ridge line fitted twice, so this hit rate on bars where neither side rounded to zero is close to the hit rate of the call itself.
The ridge intercept is the average of the clipped training moves, so a steady signed miss on later bars shows that the training span's drift was carried into the test span.
It is the money made by trading the side of zero on which the label-horizon forecast falls, under the engine's fill and exit rule with costs charged.
It relates the per-bar profit of following the sign of the label-horizon forecast to its bumpiness; zero is only an arithmetic marker because a random-direction trader still pays costs.
It shows the deepest loss run of the sign call; a ridge intercept that outweighs the feature terms can hold one side for a whole fold, which then appears here as an unhedged directional hole.
It compares winning with losing trades opened when the label-horizon forecast crossed zero, after costs; one is an arithmetic marker and not a no-skill level.
It counts the share of trades begun at a zero crossing of the forecast that closed with a profit, and must be read with the average win and loss because exits follow the engine's rule.
A small ridge forecast that hovers around zero flips sign often, and every flip is a round trip of costs that the forecast and probability scores never see.

It is the hit rate of calling up when the Gaussian tail area is at least one half, which is the model's own zero-forecast threshold and not a prior fitted on validation bars; it is read beside the majority-class accuracy of the fold.

The ridge intercept can tilt nearly every bar to one side, and averaging the hit rate over up bars and down bars shows whether the feature terms of the label-horizon line separate them once that tilt is discounted.
It condenses the four cells of the zero-threshold call into one symmetric number that stays near zero when the forecast only repeats the training drift.

It is the score on inner blocks of the training span that chose the horizon count, the reduced rank and the ridge penalty; it is a trading score and not the squared miss the ridge minimises, and it is optimistic by construction.

measuredNotMeaningful.why: With long-only off and no stop or target the engine holds a position on every bar once the first call is filled, so the share describes the engine's rule and not the ridge forecast.
Its reference is the test bars' own up share, known only in hindsight, which the Gaussian forecast could never have used, so it is not a fair reference for this model.
The closed-form ridge fit returns no training-row loss, so only the validation logarithmic loss is logged and there is no training value to subtract it from.

caveats: With the reduced rank left at zero the label-horizon coefficients are exactly those of a single ridge regression and the probability uses only that horizon's own residual variance, so the other horizons and the cross-horizon covariance change nothing in the as-run numbers; they act only when a reduced rank below the number of horizons is set or chosen by the search.

The joint outputs the specification is about, the forecasts for the other horizons and the residual covariance between horizons, are fitted and one correlation is written to the log, but none of them is scored by the engine.

The price forecast comes from a second, separately fitted copy of the same closed-form ridge, which on the same training rows gives the same label-horizon line as the copy that produces the probability.

The residual standard deviation behind the probability is estimated from training residuals of overlapping horizon moves treated as independent rows, and each target column is clipped at the outer percentiles of the training rows before the fit, so the stated spread can be narrower than the true one.
The per-fold search chooses the horizon count, the reduced rank and the penalty by the trading objective on inner blocks of the training span, not by the model's own squared miss or likelihood.
Consecutive scored bars share future bars because the label looks several bars ahead, so intervals around any score need a block bootstrap or a Newey-West variance and never a binomial interval.
The last bar of each fold exits at its close while every other exit fills at the next bar's open.
For any root other than the micro Nasdaq contract the cost per side is that contract's account figure applied as a stated assumption.
